ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In a vertical plane, a fixed circular insulating track has its center at O, with a radius $r = 0.5 \, \mathrm{m}$ and smooth inner walls. Points A and B are the lowest and highest points of the circular track, respectively. Within this region, there exists a uniform electric field directed horizontally to the right. A charged small ball (which can be treated as a point particle) with mass $m = 0.4 \, \mathrm{kg}$ and an absolute charge $q = 3 \times 10^{-5} \, \mathrm{C}$ is able to remain stationary at point C. If the ball is given an initial velocity at point C such that it can just complete a full circular motion along the inner side of the track (with the charge of the ball remaining unchanged), it is known that points C, O, and D lie on the same straight line, and the angle between this line and the vertical direction is $\theta = 37^\circ$. The gravitational acceleration is $g = 10 \, \mathrm{m/s}^2$, and the position of point C is taken as the zero potential point for both gravitational potential energy and electric potential energy ($\sin 37^\circ = 0.6$, $\cos 37^\circ = 0.8$).

1. Find the magnitude of the electric field strength; do not add any other content.
2. Find the minimum mechanical energy of the ball during its circular motion.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a circular track in a vertical plane, with the center of the circle labeled O, the highest point labeled B, and the lowest point labeled A. Multiple horizontal arrows all point to the right, indicating that the uniform electric field E is to the right. Point C is located at the lower left of the circumference, and point D is located at the upper right of the circumference. C, O, D are on the same diameter; the angle between this diameter and the vertical direction is labeled θ, and in the figure the small ball is near point C. Reasoning: The small ball can be stationary at point C, and the supporting force of the inner wall of the track on the small ball is along the direction from C to O, namely obliquely upward to the right. Gravity mg is vertically downward, therefore the electric field force must be horizontally to the left to balance the horizontal component of the supporting force. Since the direction of the electric field is to the right, the small ball is negatively charged. Let the magnitude of the electric field force be |q|E, then the equilibrium condition gives |q|E = mg tanθ. Substituting m=0.4 kg, g=10 m/s², tan37°=0.6/0.8=0.75, |q|=3×10^-5 C, gives |q|E=0.4×10×0.75=3 N, so E=3/(3×10^-5)=1.0×10^5 N/C. Combine gravity and the electric field force into a constant “effective gravity,” with magnitude F0=sqrt((mg)^2+(|q|E)^2)=sqrt(4^2+3^2)=5 N, which can also be written as F0=mg/cosθ=4/0.8=5 N. Its direction is along D pointing to C. In the equivalent vertical circular motion, the highest equivalent position is D. When just able to complete circular motion along the inner side, the supporting force at point D is zero, therefore m v_D^2/r=F0, so the kinetic energy at point D is K_D=(1/2)m v_D^2=(1/2)F0 r. Take point C as the zero point of gravitational potential energy and electric potential energy. From C to D, the effective potential energy increased against the direction of the effective force is 2F0r. Therefore the total conserved energy H_min=2F0r+(1/2)F0r=2.5F0r=2.5×5×0.5=6.25 J. The mechanical energy required by the problem is kinetic energy plus gravitational potential energy, not including electric potential energy, so M=H-U_e. For a negative charge, the electric potential energy U_e=|q|E(x-x_C), and it is maximum at the rightmost end of the circumference. From the figure, C is at the lower left, x_C=-r sinθ, and the rightmost end x=r, so the maximum horizontal displacement is r+r sinθ=r(1+sinθ)=0.5×1.6=0.8 m. Thus U_e,max=|q|E r(1+sinθ)=3×0.8=2.4 J. Therefore the minimum mechanical energy M_min=6.25-2.4=3.85 J.
